pages.name: A warm-up
pages.task: A block held under fresh water pushes aside 2 L of it. A litre of fresh water has a mass of 1 kg. What is the upthrust on the block?
pages.why: The upthrust is the weight of the water the block pushes aside. 2 L of fresh water has a mass of 2 kg. Its weight is 2 × 9.81, about 19.6 N. What the block is made of does not come into it.

pages.name: The weight above
pages.text: Pressure in a liquid comes from the weight of the liquid above. Picture a column of seawater h deep, standing on a patch of 1 m². ρ is the [[density]], the mass in each cubic metre. The column weighs ρ × h × 1 m² × g. That weight rests on 1 m², so the pressure is [[p = ρgh]]. At 10 m the probe reads about 100.6 kPa, about one atmosphere more. Fresh water is a little less dense, so each metre adds a little less.

pages.name: Any shape
pages.text: The three tanks are joined at the bottom. So the liquid settles at one level in all three. At any one depth, the probe reads the same in each. Width and shape are not in ρgh. If one bottom pressed harder, it would push liquid through the join until the levels matched. In the flaring tank, the sloping walls hold up the extra liquid. Still water presses too. It needs no flow, only weight.

pages.name: Two bases
pages.task: Two tanks of fresh water are each 2 m deep. One has a base of 0.1 m², the other 10 m². What pressure is on each bottom?
pages.why: Only the depth sets the pressure. Both bottoms are 2 m down in fresh water. So each feels 1000 × 9.81 × 2 pascals, about 19.6 kPa. The wide base carries 100 times the push, spread over 100 times the area.

pages.name: Every way at once
pages.text: At any point in a still liquid, pressure pushes every way at once. It pushes square to whatever surface it meets. So 3 m down, the probe reads about 30.2 kPa facing up, sideways or down. Its gauge counts only what the liquid adds. As with the air receiver, absolute pressure adds the air pressing on the surface, about 100 kPa.

pages.name: A hydraulic jack
pages.text: A jack shuts oil inside two joined cylinders. Push on one piston, and the oil's pressure rises by the same amount everywhere. That is [[Pascal's principle]]. 100 N on 10 cm² makes 100 kPa. That 100 kPa acts on the big 200 cm² piston, so it lifts 2,000 N. But the small piston moves 20 times as far. Pushing it 20 cm lifts the load 1 cm. Work in is 100 N × 0.2 m, or 20 J. Work out is 2,000 N × 0.01 m, also 20 J.

pages.name: A bigger jack
pages.task: A jack's small piston is 5 cm² and its big one 300 cm². You push the small one with 60 N. What load can the big one lift?
pages.why: The pressure is 60 N ÷ 0.0005 m², which is 120 kPa. The oil passes it on to the big piston. So that piston lifts 120 kPa × 0.03 m², or 3,600 N. The small piston must move 60 times as far as the load rises.

pages.name: Held under
pages.text: A 1 m cube is held with its top 2 m down. Its side pushes cancel in pairs. Its top is pushed down with about 20.1 kPa. Its bottom, 1 m deeper, is pushed up with about 30.2 kPa. On 1 m² faces, the bottom wins by about 10.1 kN. That is the [[upthrust]]. The extra pressure is ρg × 1 m, acting on 1 m². So the upthrust is ρg × 1 m³. That is the weight of 1 m³ of seawater, 1025 kg, about 10.1 kN.

pages.name: Sink or float
pages.text: Let go, and its weight meets the upthrust. Its weight depends on its own density. The upthrust depends on the liquid's. Denser than the liquid, it sinks. At 1,500 kg/m³ it weighs about 14.7 kN against 10.1 kN of upthrust. As dense as the liquid, it hovers. Less dense, it rises. A steel hull floats because its mass ÷ all the space its outside encloses is less than the water's density. [[Relative density]] is a density ÷ fresh water's. Seawater's is about 1.025.

pages.name: How deep it floats
pages.text: A cube less dense than the liquid rises. As it comes out of the surface, it pushes aside less, so the upthrust falls. It settles where the two match. The depth of its bottom is then its [[draught]]. Take a 600 kg cube. It must push aside 600 kg of seawater. That is 600 ÷ 1025, about 0.59 m³. On its 1 m² base, that is 0.59 m deep. Fresh water is less dense, so it sits deeper, at 0.60 m.

pages.name: A pontoon
pages.task: A box-shaped pontoon 4 m by 2 m has a mass of 4,000 kg. How deep does it sit in seawater?
pages.why: It sinks until it pushes aside its own mass of seawater, 4,000 kg. Its base is 4 × 2 = 8 m². So its draught is 4,000 ÷ (1025 × 8), about 0.49 m. In fresh water it would sit at 0.50 m.
